catalog_quote: [p. 26] CN is a three-register language: it lexically contrasts high (H), mid (M), and low (L) tones which stand, each to the next, in a single melodic step relationship. [...] The tone-bearing units of CN are the vowels, initial syllabic nasals (always dependent subject pronouns), and nasal verb suffixes. The registers can be combined to form contours: HM (...), HL (...), ML (...), LH (...), LM (...), LHL (...). new_statements.quote: CN is a three-register language: it lexically contrasts high (H), mid (M), and low (L) tones which stand, each to the next, in a single melodic step relationship. [p. 26] [...] It should nevertheless be clear from these indications that relative "weight" of canonic forms is used in CN in a way similar to stress in some toneless languages: the "heavier" forms such as CVCCV and CVVN are reserved for the major lexical categories and items assimilated thereto and hence signal independent terms; while the "lightest" forms, CV, N, V, are restricted to grammatical modifiers or function words and signal dependency with respect to some other term. new_statements.rule_in_words: Chamba Daka (Nnakennyaare dialect) is a three-tone language (H, M, L, plus contours and downstep) with lexical tone on every vowel; the description contains no rule for word-stress placement. Its only reference to stress is an analogy: the syllable-weight of canonic forms does the lexical-vs-grammatical signalling job that stress does in 'toneless' languages, implying CN is not such a language and does not use stress for it. No explicit claim that stress is absent or where it would fall.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonally: HM and LH contours have special realisations; LHL contour rare and merging with HL (fn. 63).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical description (uninflected base forms of nominals and verbs, citation forms); tone sandhi and utterance-final effects treated separately. The 'stress' passage concerns canonic-form weight, not prominence placement, so this is a tone-language entry without a stress rule, not a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 samb1311 'Sama Mum' = Chamba Daka / Samba Daka (ISO ccg); Raymond Boyd's site (rblanguesdafrique.info/) gives the autonym sámá mūm with ISO ccg and Glottocode samb1311 explicitly. Boyd's phonology describes the Nnakennyaare dialect of Ganye, Adamawa State, Nigeria (the lingua-franca dialect); Mapeo, Jangani, Lamja and Dirim varieties are not covered by the opened statement. Glottolog's second listed reference (Frewen 1877/78, 'Daka.. on the Zambesi') is a misattribution to a Zambezi language.

new_statements.quote: Tones: Chamba has three "registers": high, medium (or mid), and low. We represent them by marks placed above the letters which stand for the sound pronounced on the given level. Thus: báá 'to come', g~~ 'egg', dàà 'to fall' carry respectively a high, a mid, and a low tone. The representation of Chamba tone is complicated by the existence of a phenomenon which is known technically as "downstep". [p. 31] [...] Melody: the melody of each song is conditioned by the tones of its words. As a general rule, movement from a lower to a higher, or from a higher to a lower, tone requires a melodic movement in the same direction. [p. 30]

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Boyd n.d. (phonology/tonology, p. 26): three lexical tone registers H, M, L, downstep, no stress statement. The HAL PDF was obtained only with a non-browser User-Agent (hal.science's Anubis wall challenges browser UAs; the landing page and /document returned the challenge page). downloaded from https://hal.science/hal-00437971/file/bisiweeri.pdf
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chamba (Daka) is described as a three-register tone language (high, mid, low) with downstep; the paper's transcription note covers consonants, vowels, vowel length and tones only. No word-stress placement is stated and no explicit 'no stress' sentence occurs; the sole token of 'stress' (p. 6, 'stress is put on Bìsíwéérí's status as mother and wife') is rhetorical, not phonological. Song melody follows lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; downstep is marked with a slash before the affected syllable and occurs especially after grammatically derived high tones, after the modal particle é, and after high-tone verbs/clitic pronouns
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd & Fardon 1992 describes the Chamba (Daka) of Bìsíwéérí, a Muslim Chamba woman of the Jada/Mayo Ini area (then Gongola State, now Adamawa State, Nigeria), transcribed by Boyd; it does not name the dialect, but Boyd's own materials (site rblanguesdafrique.info, ISO ccg / Glottocode samb1311) describe the Nnakennyaare (Ganye) lingua-franca dialect and the same three-register system, so the paper is taken as the same language. Blench's Dakoid page covers the whole Dakoid group (Daka, Dong, Taram, Tiba), not opened.

sources.locator: III. Tonology, §1.1, p. 26 (tone statement); I. Canonic form, §3, p. 19 (stress analogy)
sources.note: Full phonology + tonology of the Nnakennyaare dialect. III Tonology 1.1 (p. 26): three-register tone language (H, M, L; contours HM, HL, ML, LH, LM, LHL; downstep). The only mention of stress is an analogy on p. 19: relative 'weight' of canonic forms 'is used in CN in a way similar to stress in some toneless languages' (heavy CVCCV/CVVN = lexical words, light CV/N/V = function words). No statement on stress placement or existence in CN itself.
